record.context_brief: Lozenge tilings of holey regular hexagons
record.original_question: Determine the number of lozenge tilings of a regular hexagon after removing two innermost unit triangles, one upward-pointing and one downward-pointing. Account for the two geometrically distinct placements in which the removed triangles are opposite or adjacent.

evidence.quote: There are two geometrically distinct ways in which we can choose to remove an upward-pointing triangle and downward-pointing triangle from these six, according to whether the triangles are opposite or adjacent.
Problem 4: Determine the number of lozenge-tilings of a regular hexagon from which two of its innermost unit triangles (one upward-pointing and one downward-pointing) have been removed.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a regular hexagon of side length $n$ drawn on the triangular lattice, so that it is naturally divided into upward- and downward-pointing unit equilateral triangles. A lozenge is the union of two unit triangles sharing an edge (one upward, one downward), and a lozenge tiling of a region is a covering by such lozenges with disjoint interiors.

The six unit triangles meeting the center of the hexagon (three upward-pointing and three downward-pointing, arranged alternately around the center) are called the innermost unit triangles. Choose one upward-pointing innermost triangle and one downward-pointing innermost triangle and delete them from the hexagon; up to symmetries of the hexagon there are exactly two geometrically distinct choices, namely:

(a) the two removed triangles are opposite (their centroids are separated by another innermost triangle), and
(b) the two removed triangles are adjacent (they share a single vertex at the center).

For each of these two cases, and for every positive integer $n$ (with $n$ chosen so that the construction makes sense, e.g., $n$ even or odd as appropriate), determine in closed form the number of lozenge tilings of the resulting region.
artifact.status_search_result: Searches indicate that Helfgott and Gessel resolved Problems 1, 2, and 10 from Propp's 1999 list of enumeration problems on tilings, but Problem 4 (the present problem) is not mentioned among those they solved. Subsequent literature on hexagons with dents, intrusions, and punctures (e.g., works of Ciucu, Krattenthaler, Lai) treats various related defect configurations, but no source found directly states a closed-form enumeration for the specific configuration of two innermost triangles (opposite or adjacent) removed. The status could not be conclusively verified from available sources.

status_evidence.claim: Helfgott–Gessel solved Propp's Problems 1, 2, 10, but Problem 4 is not listed among the solved ones.
